Empirical Research Plan  
“Do Court-Induced School‐Finance Reforms Raise Student Outcomes, and for Whom?”

────────────────────────────────────────────
1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY
────────────────────────────────────────────
Primary strategy: Staggered Difference-in-Differences (DID) with event-study
implementation à la Callaway–Sant’Anna (2021) / Sun & Abraham (2021), using the
quasi-random timing of state‐supreme-court school-finance reform (SFR)
decisions between 1971 and 2010.

Why appropriate  
• 28 states are “treated” at different calendar years; the remaining states
provide contemporaneous controls.  
• Court rulings are plausibly unrelated to year-to-year shocks in district
achievement because (i) cases are filed years earlier, (ii) decisions depend on
idiosyncratic court composition, and (iii) implementation details are delegated
to legislatures.  
• A DID/event-study design lets us recover dynamic treatment effects, test
pre-trends, and allow for heterogeneous treatment timing.

Extension / robustness: 2SLS where actual per-pupil spending is instrumented by
the interaction of (a) an indicator that a state‐year is post-reform and (b)
each district’s pre-reform poverty or property-wealth rank.  This yields a
“reduced-form” DID and an IV estimate in the same framework.

────────────────────────────────────────────
2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL
────────────────────────────────────────────
Unit of observation: District-by-cohort (e.g., 3rd‐graders in district d during
school year t).

Treatment variable  
Treated_it  = 1{State s of district i is in fiscal years ≥ first year a SFR
                formula is operative} × LowWealth_i
where LowWealth_i ≡ indicator that district i’s pre-reform property wealth
pupil falls below the state median (or use continuous percentile rank).

Control groups  
(a) Within-state, higher-wealth districts (difference-in-differences in
intensity);  
(b) Districts in never-reformed (or not-yet-reformed) states.

Treatment timing / event date  
Event date τ_s = first fiscal year in which new finance formula affects state s
aid allocations.  Event time k = t – τ_s.

No RDD used, so no running variable.

────────────────────────────────────────────
3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS
────────────────────────────────────────────
A1. Parallel Trends: In the absence of reform, outcomes of low-wealth vs.
high-wealth districts would have evolved similarly across states.  
Plausibility: Pre-reform event-study coefficients can be inspected; inclusion
of state×year economic controls (GDP, unemployment) and district fixed effects
helps.

A2. Quasi-Random Timing: Exact year a court overturns the system is
idiosyncratic and unrelated to impending shocks to student outcomes.  
Plausibility: Court dockets are long; political control of legislature, not
outcomes, determines when plaintiffs succeed.  Empirically test by regressing
pre-reform outcomes on years-to-decision.

A3. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA): Spending changes in district i do not
directly affect students in district j outside peer or migration channels.  
Plausibility: Inter-district spillovers exist but are small; we will cluster
standard errors at the state level and run robustness dropping bordering
districts.

A4. No Differential Migration correlated with reform.  
Plausibility: Court decisions are sudden; we can test for changes in enrollment
counts or demographics around τ_s.

────────────────────────────────────────────
4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATIONS
────────────────────────────────────────────
T1. Endogenous policy bundles (other education reforms accompany SFRs).  
Mitigation: Control for contemporaneous state policies (accountability laws,
teacher testing, class-size mandates) and include state×year covariates.

T2. Heterogeneous treatment timing bias in staggered DID.  
Mitigation: Use modern estimators (Callaway–Sant’Anna, Sun–Abraham) that are
robust to negative weighting.  Report group-time average treatment effects.

T3. Mean reversion or pre-trend differences.  
Mitigation: Plot 8–10 pre-reform years in event study; formally test joint
significance of leads.  If violated, implement synthetic control
pre-weighting as a robustness check.

────────────────────────────────────────────
5. R CODE OUTLINE
────────────────────────────────────────────
```r
# Packages
library(data.table)      # fast data handling
library(fixest)          # high-dim FE & DID
library(did)             # Callaway–Sant’Anna
library(readr)

# 1. Load data -------------------------------------------------------------
district <- fread("district_panel_1970_2018.csv")  # 1 row per dist-year

# 2. Variable construction -------------------------------------------------
district[, post  := year >= reform_year]                 # reform year τ_s
district[, low   := as.integer(pre_wealth_pctile < 50)]  # bottom half wealth
district[, treat := post * low]                          # DID interaction
district[, event_time := year - reform_year]             # for event study

# Outcome examples
# standardised 4th-grade math z-score
# high_school_grad_rate, adult_wage_age25_35 etc.

# 3. Main two-way FE DID ---------------------------------------------------
did_main <- feols(outcome_z ~ treat | district + state_year,
                  data = district, cluster = "state")
summary(did_main)

# 4. Event-study (Sun & Abraham) ------------------------------------------
event_spec <- feols(outcome_z ~ sunab(reform_year, year, ref.p = -1) |
                                  district + state_year,
                    data = district, cluster = "state")
iplot(event_spec)              # visually inspect leads/lags

# 5. Callaway–Sant’Anna ATT -----------------------------------------------
cs <- att_gt(yname = "outcome_z",
             gname = "reform_year",
             idname = "district",
             tname = "year",
             xformla = ~ low,
             data = district,
             panel = TRUE,
             clustervars = "state")
aggte_cs <- aggte(cs, type = "dynamic")
ggdid(aggte_cs)

# 6. IV robustness: 2SLS of spending on outcomes --------------------------
district[, spend_iv := post * low]   # first-stage instrument
iv_res <- feols(outcome_z ~ 1 | spend_pc ~ spend_iv |
                district + state_year,
                data = district, cluster = "state")
summary(iv_res)

# 7. Placebo check: shift pseudo-reform 10y earlier -----------------------
district[, pseudo_post := (year >= (reform_year - 10))]
district[, pseudo_treat := pseudo_post * low]
placebo <- feols(outcome_z ~ pseudo_treat |
                 district + state_year,
                 data = district, cluster = "state")
summary(placebo)
```

────────────────────────────────────────────
6. EXPECTED RESULTS
────────────────────────────────────────────
Economic theory (education production plus credit constraints) predicts
positive marginal returns for low-income students.  Prior quasi-experimental
evidence suggests:

• $1,000 (2018$) sustained per-pupil increase for 4–6 years  
   → +0.04σ in math/reading,  
   → +2–3 p.p. higher high-school graduation,  
   → +2 % higher adult wages (Age 25–45).  

Effects should be 50–100 % larger in the bottom income tercile and near zero
for top tercile.

────────────────────────────────────────────
7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT
────────────────────────────────────────────
(1 = clearly satisfied, 0 = questionable)

C1. Credible source of exogenous variation (court timing) …… 1  
C2. Parallel pre-trends visually & statistically verified …… 0.8  
C3. No spillovers or interference violations …………………… 0.7  
C4. Correct inference & treatment-timing estimator ………… 1  
C5. Robustness to alternative specifications ………………… 1  

Overall score ≈ 4.5 / 5 — high but not perfect validity.

────────────────────────────────────────────
End of Research Plan
